p: Custer rode to the front of his brigade. He turned to his Wolverines.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 7 of 12

p: He spurred his horse directly at the Confederate advance. The Michigan Brigade came with him.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 8 of 12

p: The two lines met at a full gallop in the largest cavalry engagement of the Gettysburg campaign. Men sabre'd each other at close range, horses went down, the lines interpenetrated and dissolved into a melee of individual combats across a half-mile front. Hampton was wounded — a sabre cut to the head.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 9 of 12

p: When it was over, Stuart's cavalry fell back. The Union rear was secure.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
p.short: Site vignette “Custer at East Cavalry Field”, paragraph 10 of 12

p: On Cemetery Ridge, the last of Pickett's men were streaming back from The Angle.

p: Elon Farnsworth had been a general for eight days.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: He had the promotion because he was a good cavalry officer and because his uncle was an influential congressman and because Pleasonton was promoting young men he trusted. Eight days — long enough to receive the commission, pin on the stars, and die.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Farnsworth looked at the ground ahead. It was a nightmare of boulders and fencing and rocky terrain, defended by Law's Confederate infantry and the dismounted men of Robertson's Texas Brigade. Cavalry — even the best cavalry — could not charge formed infantry over ground like that.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)
Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Kilpatrick, in the accounts that survive, challenged his courage. The exact words are disputed, but the meaning was clear: charge, or be thought a coward.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: Farnsworth's face went white. Then he said something that the men nearby remembered for the rest of their lives — an expression of outrage, of contempt, and of acceptance, all in one breath. He would lead the charge himself.

p.author_line: Ask the Historian site records (narrative vignette)

p: 'If you order the charge, I will lead it,' he said. 'But if we go in there it will be a charge of death.'
